Chess Olympiad dataset: descriptive statistics¶

General overview of the Olympiad database (2010–2026, Open and Women's sections): who played, how strong they were, how games ended, how long they lasted, and what clock data exists.

Sources: The Week in Chess (all games, teams, boards, ratings, results and the official moves) and Lichess broadcasts (clock readings and engine evaluations, attached to those moves, 2018 onwards). 2020 and 2021 are excluded because those Olympiads were online rapid events.

Definitions used throughout

  • Played game: a game with a 1-0, ½-½ or 0-1 result and recorded moves. Games with no moves are left out, and so are decisive games of fewer than 5 moves, which are almost certainly forfeits.
  • Rated game: a played game where both players have a rating in the source file.
  • Team average rating: the mean rating of a team's players over the games they played in that Olympiad, so a player with more games counts more. Unrated players are left out of the mean.

To rerun: start the PostgreSQL server, set DATABASE_URL if it differs from the default below, and choose Run All.

import os

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import psycopg
from IPython.display import display
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter, PercentFormatter

%config InlineBackend.figure_format = "retina"

DSN = os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL", "postgresql://chess:chess@localhost:5432/chess_olympiad")


def query(sql):
    with psycopg.connect(DSN) as conn:
        cur = conn.execute(sql)
        return pd.DataFrame(cur.fetchall(), columns=[d.name for d in cur.description])

thousands = FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v / 1000:g}K" if v >= 1000 else f"{v:g}")


def legend_on_top(ax, ncol=4):
    ax.legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.0), ncol=ncol, borderaxespad=0, handlelength=1.4, columnspacing=1.4)


def grouped_columns(ax, table, colors, width=0.3):
    """Columns for each row of `table`, one group per index value, one colour per column."""
    x = np.arange(len(table))
    n = table.shape[1]
    for i, col in enumerate(table.columns):
        ax.bar(x + (i - (n - 1) / 2) * width, table[col], width, label=col, color=colors[col],
               edgecolor=SURFACE, linewidth=1.5)
    ax.set_xticks(x, table.index.astype(str))


def rate_with_ci(frame, by, flag):
    """Share (%) of `flag` for each group, with a 95% Wilson interval (lo, hi).
    The interval treats games as independent. Games of the same match and team are not,
    so it is somewhat too narrow: read it as a guide to sample size, not as a test."""
    out = frame.groupby(by, observed=True)[flag].agg(rate="mean", n="size").reset_index()
    z = 1.96
    centre = (out["rate"] + z**2 / (2 * out["n"])) / (1 + z**2 / out["n"])
    half = z * np.sqrt(out["rate"] * (1 - out["rate"]) / out["n"] + z**2 / (4 * out["n"] ** 2)) / (1 + z**2 / out["n"])
    out["lo"], out["hi"] = (centre - half) * 100, (centre + half) * 100
    out["rate"] *= 100
    return out


def line_with_band(ax, x, y, lo, hi, color, label, marker=None):
    ax.fill_between(x, lo, hi, color=color, alpha=0.12, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot(x, y, color=color, label=label, marker=marker, markersize=6,
            markeredgecolor=SURFACE, markeredgewidth=1.5)

1. Dataset at a glance¶

In [2]:
games = query("""
    SELECT g.game_id, g.match_id, e.year, initcap(e.section) AS section, m.round, m.match_no, g.board,
           g.white_id, g.black_id, tw.name AS white_team, tb.name AS black_team,
           NULLIF(g.white_elo, 0) AS white_elo, NULLIF(g.black_elo, 0) AS black_elo,
           g.white_title, g.black_title, g.result, g.white_score::float8 AS white_score,
           g.eco, g.n_plies, g.board_source, g.lichess_url IS NOT NULL AS has_lichess,
           g.has_clocks, g.clock_ok, g.end_elapsed_s
    FROM games g
    JOIN matches m USING (match_id)
    JOIN events e USING (event_id)
    LEFT JOIN teams tw ON tw.team_id = g.white_team_id
    LEFT JOIN teams tb ON tb.team_id = g.black_team_id
""")
for col in ["white_elo", "black_elo", "white_score", "end_elapsed_s", "board"]:
    games[col] = pd.to_numeric(games[col], errors="coerce")

moves_played = np.ceil(games.n_plies / 2)
likely_forfeit = (moves_played < 5) & games.result.isin(["1-0", "0-1"])
played = games[(games.n_plies > 0) & games.result.isin(["1-0", "1/2-1/2", "0-1"]) & ~likely_forfeit].copy()
played["outcome"] = played.result.map({"1-0": "White win", "1/2-1/2": "Draw", "0-1": "Black win"})
played["draw"] = played.result.eq("1/2-1/2")
played["moves"] = np.ceil(played.n_plies / 2)

rated = played.dropna(subset=["white_elo", "black_elo"]).copy()
rated["avg_elo"] = (rated.white_elo + rated.black_elo) / 2
rated["elo_diff"] = rated.white_elo - rated.black_elo
rated["elo_gap"] = rated.elo_diff.abs()

# One row per player per game
appearances = pd.concat([
    played[["year", "section", "round", "match_id", "board", "white_id", "white_team", "white_elo", "white_title"]]
    .set_axis(["year", "section", "round", "match_id", "board", "player", "team", "elo", "title"], axis=1),
    played[["year", "section", "round", "match_id", "board", "black_id", "black_team", "black_elo", "black_title"]]
    .set_axis(["year", "section", "round", "match_id", "board", "player", "team", "elo", "title"], axis=1),
], ignore_index=True)

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Games": [len(games)],
    "Played games": [len(played)],
    "Rated games": [len(rated)],
    "Games with clock data": [int(games.has_clocks.sum())],
    "Games with clock data that passes all checks": [int(games.clock_ok.sum())],
    "Matches": [games.match_id.nunique()],
    "Olympiads": [games.year.nunique()],
    "Player records": [pd.concat([games.white_id, games.black_id]).nunique()],
}).T.rename(columns={0: "Count"})
display(summary.style.format("{:,}"))

overview = (
    games.groupby(["year", "section"])
    .agg(matches=("match_id", "nunique"), games=("game_id", "size"), rounds=("round", "max"),
         with_clocks=("has_clocks", "sum"))
    .join(appearances.groupby(["year", "section"]).agg(teams=("team", "nunique"), players=("player", "nunique")))
    .join(played.groupby(["year", "section"]).size().rename("played"))
    .join(rated.groupby(["year", "section"]).size().rename("rated"))
)
overview["rated_%"] = (overview.rated / overview.played * 100).round(1)
overview["clocks_%"] = (overview.with_clocks / overview.games * 100).round(1)
overview = overview[["rounds", "teams", "players", "matches", "games", "played", "rated", "rated_%", "with_clocks", "clocks_%"]]
display(overview)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
grouped_columns(ax, overview.games.unstack("section")[SECTIONS], SECTION_COLOR)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
ax.set_ylabel("Games")
ax.set_title("Games per Olympiad", pad=30)
legend_on_top(ax)
plt.show()

What this shows

  • The Olympiad has grown from 5,746 games in 2010 to 8,645 in 2026. Of all 56,436 games, 55,796 count as played under the definition above.
  • Both players have a rating in 79–94% of played Open games per Olympiad, and in 74–89% of Women's games.
  • Clock data starts in 2018, covering 75–78% of games that year and 94–99% from 2022. The 2018 gap is not random: in rounds 1–4 only the top 32 tables were broadcast (section 6).
  • Teams and players are counted only if they played at least one game under this definition, so these totals can be slightly below the official entry lists.

2. Player ratings¶

Each point below counts one player in one game. FIDE compressed ratings below 2000 in March 2024, which raised low ratings, so ratings below about 2000 are not directly comparable before and after that date.

What this shows

  • The median Open rating fell from 2,416 in 2010 to 2,203 in 2026, and the Women's median from 2,122 to 1,905. The Women's section sits about 300 points lower throughout. These figures cover rated players only, so part of the fall may reflect more low-rated players having a FIDE rating.
  • The Women's lower quartile jumps from 1,560 in 2022 to 1,726 in 2024, which fits the 2024 rating compression.
  • Mean rating falls steadily from board 1 to board 4: 2,337 to 2,205 in the Open and 2,053 to 1,890 in the Women's section.
  • Grandmasters make up 27.8% of Open entries. In the Women's section, 2.4% hold the GM title and 41.4% have no title listed.

3. Team strength¶

In [7]:
team_event = (
    appearances.groupby(["year", "section", "team"])
    .agg(avg_rating=("elo", "mean"), player_games=("elo", "size"), rated_games=("elo", "count"), players=("player", "nunique"))
    .reset_index()
)
team_event["rated_share"] = team_event.rated_games / team_event.player_games
# Averages built from few rated games say little about the team
teams = team_event[(team_event.rated_share >= 0.5) & (team_event.rated_games >= 10)].copy()


def strongest(group):
    ordered = group.sort_values("avg_rating")
    return pd.Series({
        "teams": len(group),
        "mean": round(group.avg_rating.mean()),
        "median": round(group.avg_rating.median()),
        "std": round(group.avg_rating.std()),
        "strongest": f"{ordered.team.iloc[-1]} ({ordered.avg_rating.iloc[-1]:.0f})",
        "weakest": f"{ordered.team.iloc[0]} ({ordered.avg_rating.iloc[0]:.0f})",
    })


team_table = pd.DataFrame({key: strongest(group) for key, group in teams.groupby(["year", "section"])}).T
team_table.index.names = ["year", "section"]
display(team_table)
print(f"Teams left out for too few rated games: {len(team_event) - len(teams)} of {len(team_event)}")

latest = max(years)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
for ax, section in zip(axes, SECTIONS):
    top = teams[(teams.year == latest) & (teams.section == section)].nlargest(10, "avg_rating").iloc[::-1]
    ax.scatter(top.avg_rating, top.team, s=70, color=SECTION_COLOR[section], edgecolor=SURFACE, linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
    ax.set_xlim(top.avg_rating.min() - 20, top.avg_rating.max() + 35)
    for name, value in zip(top.team, top.avg_rating):
        ax.text(value + 9, name, f"{value:.0f}", va="center", color=INK_2, fontsize=9.5)
    ax.grid(axis="y")
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.set_xlabel("Team average rating")
    ax.set_title(section)
fig.suptitle(f"Ten highest team average ratings, {latest}", x=0.01, ha="left",
             fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

How even are the matches?¶

The Olympiad is a Swiss tournament: after the first round, teams meet others with similar scores. The rating gap should therefore shrink after early rounds.

The match-level figures use only matches with four games on boards 1 to 4. In 39 matches a game is missing from the source files.

In [10]:
team_of = games.melt(id_vars="match_id", value_vars=["white_team", "black_team"], value_name="team")
check = (
    games.groupby("match_id")
    .agg(n=("game_id", "size"), boards=("board", lambda b: b.dropna().nunique()), year=("year", "first"),
         section=("section", "first"), round=("round", "first"))
    .join(team_of.groupby("match_id").team.nunique().rename("n_teams"))
)
clean_ids = check[(check.n == 4) & (check.boards == 4) & (check.n_teams == 2)].index

lookup = teams.set_index(["year", "section", "team"]).avg_rating
sides = games[games.match_id.isin(clean_ids) & games.board.eq(1)][["match_id", "year", "section", "round", "white_team", "black_team"]].copy()
sides["white_avg"] = lookup.reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(sides[["year", "section", "white_team"]])).values
sides["black_avg"] = lookup.reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(sides[["year", "section", "black_team"]])).values
sides["team_gap"] = (sides.white_avg - sides.black_avg).abs()
gap_by_round = sides.dropna(subset=["team_gap"]).groupby(["round", "section"]).team_gap.median().unstack()[SECTIONS]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for section in SECTIONS:
    ax.plot(gap_by_round.index, gap_by_round[section], color=SECTION_COLOR[section], marker="o", markersize=7,
            markeredgecolor=SURFACE, markeredgewidth=1.5, label=section)
ax.set_xticks(gap_by_round.index)
ax.set_ylim(0, None)
ax.set_xlabel("Round")
ax.set_ylabel("Median rating gap between teams")
ax.set_title("Team rating gap by round", pad=30)
legend_on_top(ax)
plt.show()

match_games = games[games.match_id.isin(clean_ids) & games.result.isin(["1-0", "1/2-1/2", "0-1"])].copy()
first_board = games[games.match_id.isin(clean_ids) & games.board.eq(1)].set_index("match_id")
match_games["team_a"] = match_games.match_id.map(first_board.white_team)
match_games["a_points"] = np.where(match_games.white_team == match_games.team_a, match_games.white_score, 1 - match_games.white_score)
match_games["a_elo"] = np.where(match_games.white_team == match_games.team_a, match_games.white_elo, match_games.black_elo)
match_games["b_elo"] = np.where(match_games.white_team == match_games.team_a, match_games.black_elo, match_games.white_elo)

matches = match_games.groupby("match_id").agg(
    year=("year", "first"), section=("section", "first"), scored=("a_points", "size"), a=("a_points", "sum"),
    a_lineup=("a_elo", "mean"), b_lineup=("b_elo", "mean"), a_rated=("a_elo", "count"), b_rated=("b_elo", "count"))
matches = matches[matches.scored == 4].copy()
matches["winner_points"] = np.maximum(matches.a, 4 - matches.a)

both = matches[(matches.a_rated == 4) & (matches.b_rated == 4)].copy()
both["gap"] = (both.a_lineup - both.b_lineup).abs()
stronger_is_a = both.a_lineup >= both.b_lineup
stronger_points = np.where(stronger_is_a, both.a, 4 - both.a)
both["outcome"] = np.select([stronger_points > 2, stronger_points == 2], ["Stronger team won", "Match drawn"], "Weaker team won")
gap_labels = ["0–25", "25–50", "50–100", "100–150", "150–200", "200–300", "300+"]
both["gap_bin"] = pd.cut(both.gap, [0, 25, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, np.inf], labels=gap_labels, include_lowest=True)
share = both.groupby("gap_bin", observed=True).outcome.value_counts(normalize=True).unstack().fillna(0) * 100
outcomes = ["Stronger team won", "Match drawn", "Weaker team won"]

What this shows

  • The strongest Open team averages 2,743–2,764 in every Olympiad, while the mean team fell from 2,382 to 2,181. The field has widened below a stable top.
  • The strongest Women's team ranges from 2,450 to 2,534, and the mean team fell from 2,092 to 1,911.
  • Swiss pairing narrows the matches quickly. The median team rating gap in the Open falls from 499 in round 1 to 113 in round 11, and in the Women's section from 526 to 130. Most of that happens in the first three rounds.
  • About 13% of matches finish 2–2, and 25.5% of Open and 21.9% of Women's matches finish 2½–1½. Whitewashes (4–0) make up 19.9% and 24.8%.
  • Ratings predict match results well but not perfectly. With a gap under 25 points, the stronger team wins 40.4% of matches and the weaker team 34.2%. At 300 points or more, the stronger team wins 96.7%.

What this shows

  • The Open draw rate fell from 32.0% in 2010 to between 23% and 27% from 2014. The Women's rate stays between 18.6% and 23.8%.
  • Draws depend heavily on rating level. Below an average rating of 2000, about 17% of games are drawn in both sections. In the Open this reaches 60.6% at 2700–2800, and in the Women's section 58.7% at 2500–2600 (only 121 games).
  • Above 2000, Women's games at the same rating level are drawn more often than Open games: 39.4% against 23.7% at 2300–2400. This is a raw comparison with nothing controlled. A 2300–2400 game is a top-board game between strong teams in the Women's section and a middle-board game in the Open, so the two groups differ in more than the section.
  • Draws also depend on how evenly matched the players are. The Open draw rate falls from 42.3% with a gap under 25 points to 6.8% at 400 or more, and the Women's rate from 33.0% to 6.2%.
  • White scores 53.5% in closely matched games. White's results run above the Elo formula when White is about equal or lower rated, and match it when White is much stronger.
  • The shaded bands are 95% Wilson intervals that treat games as independent. Games of the same match and team are not, so the bands are somewhat too narrow.
  • Draw rates fall slightly from board 1 to board 4. They are very low in round 1 (6.8% Open, 3.8% Women's), when mismatches are largest, and settle at about 26–32% and 20–25% from round 3.

What this shows

  • The median game lasts 41–43 moves when decisive and 46–47 when drawn. Median length barely changes with rating level.
  • Draws jump sharply at move 30. There are 76 draws at exactly move 29 and 502 at move 30. In 2010, 24.5% of Open and 19.8% of Women's draws ended before move 30, compared with only 3–7% from 2012. The Olympiad regulations forbid agreeing a draw before Black's 30th move. The rule was introduced at Dresden 2008 and is in the 2022 and 2024 regulations. The 2010 figure suggests it was not applied in Khanty-Mansiysk, which should be confirmed in the 2010 regulations. It matters when comparing draw rates over time, including the higher 2010 Open figure above.
  • 1.e4 is White's most common first move, at 46.3% in the Open and 55.3% in the Women's section. No single ECO code accounts for more than about 3% of games.

6. Clock and engine data¶

Clock readings exist only where a Lichess broadcast game could be matched, so from 2018 onwards. The data records the time left after each move, not timestamps. Thinking time and game duration are calculated from those readings.

Two things about the clocks matter for this section:

  • The 30 minutes after move 40. In 2018 the clocks counted moves and added the 30 minutes when a player completed move 40. From 2022 the clocks did not count moves. They add the 30 minutes to both clocks at the moment the first player's time runs out, and not at all if neither player runs out. Time left below is the clock reading plus the 30 minutes from move 40 on, for as long as the clock does not show them yet, so that all years mean the same thing.
  • Checks. Readings that cannot be right are left out: 0:00:00, a clock that repeats the same time move after move, and a reading contradicted by the ones around it. Duration, thinking time and time left use only the games that pass all checks: no unexplained jump of a clock, no single move above 45 minutes, and a reading on the last move.
In [22]:
coverage = query("""
    SELECT e.year, initcap(e.section) AS section,
           count(*) AS moves,
           count(mv.clock_s) AS with_clock,
           count(mv.eval_cp) + count(mv.eval_mate) AS with_eval
    FROM moves mv
    JOIN games g USING (game_id)
    JOIN matches m USING (match_id)
    JOIN events e USING (event_id)
    GROUP BY 1, 2
    ORDER BY 1, 2
""").astype({"moves": int, "with_clock": int, "with_eval": int}).set_index(["year", "section"])
coverage["clock_%"] = (coverage.with_clock / coverage.moves * 100).round(1)
coverage["eval_%"] = (coverage.with_eval / coverage.moves * 100).round(1)

# Durations use the games whose clock data passes all checks (see section 7)
clocked = played[played.clock_ok & played.end_elapsed_s.notna()].copy()
clocked["hours"] = clocked.end_elapsed_s / 3600
# Each player has at most 2 hours plus 30 s per move, so nothing should be longer than this
limit = 2 * (7200 + 30 * clocked.moves)

# When does the 30-minute bonus first appear on a clock? Games of 45 moves or more.
bonus = query("""
    SELECT e.year, g.game_id, min(mv.move_no) FILTER (WHERE mv.bonus_added) AS bonus_move
    FROM games g
    JOIN matches m USING (match_id)
    JOIN events e USING (event_id)
    JOIN moves mv USING (game_id)
    WHERE g.clock_ok AND g.n_plies >= 89
    GROUP BY 1, 2
""")
when = ["Before move 40", "At move 40", "Moves 41–45", "Move 46 or later", "Never"]
bonus["shown"] = pd.cut(bonus.bonus_move.astype(float), [0, 39, 40, 45, 999], labels=when[:4]).astype(object).fillna("Never")
bonus_table = (bonus.groupby("year").shown.value_counts(normalize=True).unstack().reindex(columns=when).fillna(0) * 100).round(1)
bonus_table["games"] = bonus.groupby("year").size()
display(bonus_table.rename_axis(index="Year", columns="Bonus first shown (% of games)"))

What this shows

  • Engine evaluations cover about half of moves in 2018, 71–87% in 2022, and at least 96% in 2024 and 2026.
  • The 2018 clock data is not a random sample. Rounds 1–4 have it for the top 32 tables only; rounds 5–11 have it for nearly all tables.
  • The median game lasts about 3.4 hours, and the middle half of games about 2.8–4.1 hours. Time after the last move is not recorded, so true durations are slightly longer.
  • Players move quickly in the opening (a median of 7–8 seconds on move 1), then think longest around move 15 (160 seconds in the Open, 185 in the Women's section).
  • Median thinking time falls to about 40 seconds by move 40, rises to 66–77 seconds on move 41 once the time control has passed, then declines to about 20 seconds by move 80.
  • Time pressure before move 40 is common. After move 39 the median player has about 6 minutes left in the Open and under 5 in the Women's section.
  • After move 40 the median player has about 35 minutes, 21–22 minutes after move 50 and 11–12 after move 60.
  • The last table shows the two clock settings. In 2018 the 30 minutes appear at move 40 in 94% of long games. From 2022 they appear at moves 41–45 in 67–73%, later in about 9%, and never in 18–23%. In those games neither player used up the first period. This is how the clocks work, not missing data.
  • 1,098 of the 28,549 played games with clock data fail a check and are left out of this section.

7. Data limitations¶

Points to keep in mind when reading these figures:

  • Team names vary across years. 2010 uses country codes (GER) and later years use full names, with some spelling changes. Each Olympiad is internally consistent, so per-Olympiad team statistics are unaffected, but teams should not be tracked across years by name until these are standardised.
  • Ratings are as listed in the game files. The FIDE rating compression of March 2024 affects comparisons below about 2000 across years.
  • Moves are the official score. Clock readings and evaluations from the broadcast are attached to the official moves. Moves that only the broadcast has, mostly kings placed in the centre after the game, are not stored.
  • Labels in the source files were repaired where they contradict each other. Matches are formed from the two teams, not from the table number in the file, which is wrong for some games (in 2024 in every round). 40 board numbers were worked out from the colours. The pipeline prints every repair when it loads the data.
  • The 30-minute bonus. From 2022 it goes on both clocks when the first player's time runs out, and never if neither runs out, which is about one long game in five. To compare time left across years use time_left_s, not clock_s.
  • Clock reconstruction. Elapsed time is the time both players have used according to their clocks. It does not include arbiter stoppages or the time between the last move and the end of the game, so games that end within about 3 minutes of each other should not be ordered by finishing time. clock_ok marks the games that pass all checks.
